title: Biodiversity, Classification and Sampling
seo_title: Year 11 Biology: Biodiversity and Classification Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Biodiversity at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels; classification systems, binomial nomenclature and dichotomous keys; sampling with quadrats, transects and capture–recapture; and diversity indices. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 1: Biodiversity and the interconnectedness of life)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Biology worksheets on biodiversity: genetic, species and ecosystem diversity, the three domains, binomial names, keys, quadrats, capture–recapture and Simpson's index. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Simpson's index: D = 1 − Σn(n − 1) ÷ N(N − 1). Closer to 1 = more diverse.
body_html:
How to think about it

Biodiversity is the variety of life at three levels: genetic (alleles within a species), species (how many species and how evenly they are spread) and ecosystem (the variety of habitats). Australia's long isolation gives it very high endemism.

Organisms are grouped into three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) and then kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Each species has a binomial name such as Phascolarctos cinereus.

Sample plants with random quadrats and gradients with transects; estimate mobile animals with capture–mark–recapture, N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂.

Example

Quadrats: A 10, B 5, C 5. Find Simpson's index.

N = 20, Σn(n − 1) = 90 + 20 + 20 = 130

D = 1 − 130 ÷ (20 × 19)

Answer: 0.658

Example

30 skinks marked; later 20 caught, 4 marked. Population?

N = 30 × 20 ÷ 4

Answer: 150

Common mistakes

  • Thinking more individuals means more diversity: evenness matters too.
  • Writing the binomial name with a capital letter for the species.
  • Placing quadrats where the plants look interesting instead of at random.

faq.q: What does Simpson's index tell you?
faq.a: How diverse a community is, from 0 (one species) towards 1 (many species with similar numbers). It combines richness and evenness.

faq.q: Why is Australian biodiversity so unusual?
faq.a: Australia was isolated for tens of millions of years, so most of its mammals, reptiles and flowering plants are endemic: found nowhere else.

items.q: Why is high genetic diversity important to a population?
c: some individuals are more likely to survive a new disease or change
it increases the population's size immediately
items.e: Variation is the raw material for natural selection.

items.q: How have feral cats and red foxes affected Australian mammals?
c: they have caused the extinction of many small and medium-sized mammals
they have increased native mammal numbers
items.e: Australia has the world's worst modern rate of mammal extinction.

items.q: What is co-extinction?
c: the birth of a new species
the extinction of a species that depends on another species that has become extinct
items.e: e.g. a parasite dying with its host.

items.q: How does species diversity change from the equator to the poles?
c: it is highest at the poles
items.e: The tropics are the richest.

items.q: What is ecosystem diversity?
c: the variety of habitats, communities and ecological processes in a region
the variety of alleles in one species
the size of the largest ecosystem
the number of species in one quadrat
items.e: A region with reef, mangrove and seagrass has high ecosystem diversity.

items.q: Which statement about Australia's biodiversity is correct?
c: all its species arrived after European settlement
it has fewer endemic species than most countries
most of its mammals, reptiles and flowering plants are found nowhere else
items.e: Long isolation after Gondwana broke up led to high endemism.

items.q: What is biodiversity?
c: the number of animals in an area
the variety of life at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels
the number of endangered species in a country
the total mass of plants in an ecosystem
items.e: Biodiversity includes genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.

items.q: Which Australian region is a recognised global biodiversity hotspot?
items.e: It has thousands of endemic plant species.

items.q: Which of these is the greatest current threat to Australian biodiversity?
items.e: Land clearing, foxes, cats and weeds have driven many extinctions.

items.q: Tasmanian devils have very low genetic diversity. Why has this made devil facial tumour disease worse?
c: the disease is caused by a mutation in the climate
their immune systems do not recognise tumour cells from other devils as foreign
low diversity makes them grow too fast
items.e: Similar genes mean the tumour cells are not rejected.

items.q: Why does Australia have so many endemic species?
c: it was isolated for tens of millions of years after it separated from Gondwana
it has the coldest climate on Earth
it has the most rainfall of any continent
items.e: Isolation allowed lineages such as marsupials to diversify.

items.q: Which is an example of ecosystem diversity on the Queensland coast?
c: coral reef, seagrass meadow, mangrove forest and rainforest in one region
one crop planted over a large area
different colours of one species of butterfly
items.e: Ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems.

items.q: What are sacred groves?
c: forest patches protected by local communities for religious reasons
items.e: Found in Meghalaya, Rajasthan, the Western Ghats and elsewhere.

items.q: What is species evenness?
c: the total biomass of the community
how similar the population sizes of the different species are
the number of individuals of the rarest species
items.e: A community where one species dominates has low evenness.

items.q: What is a biodiversity hotspot?
c: a place where a single species is very common
a region with very many endemic species that has lost much of its original habitat
items.e: South-west Western Australia is a recognised hotspot.

items.q: What does the IUCN Red List record?
c: the conservation status of species and those threatened with extinction
items.e: Updated regularly.

items.q: What is species diversity?
c: the variety of alleles in a population
the number of individuals of one species
the number of species in an area and how evenly the individuals are spread among them
the variety of ecosystems in a region
items.e: Species diversity takes in richness and evenness.

items.q: What is species richness?
c: the number of different species in an area
how evenly individuals are spread among species
items.e: Richness counts species; evenness compares their numbers.

items.q: Two sites each have 5 species. At site A each species has about 20 individuals; at site B one species has 90 and the rest have 2 or 3. Which is more diverse?
c: site B, because it has more individuals of one species
site A, because it has the same richness and higher evenness
they are equally diverse because richness is the same
site B, because dominance means a healthier community
items.e: Same richness, higher evenness = higher diversity.

items.q: What is the most species-rich group of animals?
items.e: More than 70% of all recorded animal species.

items.q: What is the common name of Pisum sativum?
items.e: Pisum sativum: pea.

items.q: In Macropus giganteus (eastern grey kangaroo), what does Macropus name?
items.e: The first word of a binomial name is the genus.

items.q: What is the binomial name of the koala?
items.e: Genus capitalised, species lower case, both in italics.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for dog?
items.e: Canis familiaris: dog.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for cotton?
items.e: Gossypium hirsutum: cotton.

items.q: In Mangifera indica, what does 'indica' stand for?
items.e: Mangifera is the genus.

items.q: A cladogram shows that kangaroos and koalas share a more recent common ancestor than kangaroos and platypuses. What does this mean?
c: kangaroos and platypuses are the same species
kangaroos are more closely related to koalas than to platypuses
items.e: A more recent common ancestor means a closer relationship.

items.q: What is the common name of Triticum aestivum?
items.e: Triticum aestivum: wheat.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below kingdom?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for maize?
items.e: Zea mays: maize.

items.q: Why is DNA sequencing now used to classify organisms?
c: it removes the need for names
it is cheaper than looking at organisms
it shows relationships that are hidden by similar or different body shapes
items.e: Convergent evolution can make unrelated organisms look alike.

items.q: Which domain includes many organisms that live in extreme environments such as hot springs?
items.e: Archaea are prokaryotes but differ from bacteria in their membranes and rRNA.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly above phylum?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: Why do scientists use binomial names rather than common names?
c: each species has one unique name understood worldwide
binomial names describe the colour of the species
items.e: A ‘magpie’ in Australia and in Europe are different birds.

items.q: What is the common name of Felis catus?
items.e: Felis catus: cat.

items.q: Which domain includes all organisms with a nucleus?
items.e: Animals, plants, fungi and protists are eukaryotes.

items.q: Which category includes related genera?
items.e: e.g. Felidae includes Panthera and Felis.

items.q: Which statement about classification is correct?
c: organisms in the same kingdom are always the same species
organisms in the same genus are more closely related than organisms in the same order
a class is smaller than a genus
items.e: Lower taxa share more features.

items.q: What does a dichotomous key do?
c: shows how energy flows through an ecosystem
measures the size of a population
identifies organisms by a series of choices between two features
lists organisms in order of size
items.e: Each step splits the group into two.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for tiger?
items.e: Panthera tigris: tiger.

items.q: Why are quadrats placed at random?
c: to make sure the rarest species is found
so each quadrat has the same number of species
to avoid bias in choosing where to sample
items.e: Random positions come from random-number coordinates.

items.q: When is a quadrat the best sampling method?
c: for animals that are active only at night
for plants or slow-moving animals in an area
items.e: Quadrats sample a fixed area.

items.q: Quadrats of 0.50 m² are placed at random in a 100 m² field. The mean is 2.5 daisies per quadrat. Estimate the total number of daisies.
20 voles are caught, marked and released. Later 40 are caught and 4 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
Which abiotic factor is measured with a light meter on a transect?
items.e: Abiotic data help explain the pattern of organisms.

items.q: Quadrats of 0.50 m² are placed at random in a 500 m² field. The mean is 4.0 daisies per quadrat. Estimate the total number of daisies.
Quadrats of 0.25 m² are placed at random in a 100 m² field. The mean is 8.4 dandelions per quadrat. Estimate the total number of dandelions.
A quadrat divided into 50 squares has a species in 12 of them. Calculate the percentage cover (frequency).
A student uses a pitfall trap. What is it for?
items.e: Pitfall traps are checked often so animals are not harmed.

items.q: Quadrats of 0.50 m² are placed at random in a 1000 m² field. The mean is 2.5 daisies per quadrat. Estimate the total number of daisies.
Which tool is used to sample invertebrates in long grass?
items.e: Sweep nets are swung through vegetation.

items.q: What is a niche?
c: the role of a species in its habitat
the place where an organism lives
all the species in an area
items.e: Two species cannot share exactly the same niche.

items.q: What is succession?
c: a gradual change in the species in an area over time
items.e: Pioneer species change the conditions for others.

items.q: What does percentage cover measure?
c: the number of individuals in a quadrat
the number of species in the area
the proportion of a quadrat's area covered by one species
the height of the tallest plant
items.e: Useful for grasses and mosses that are hard to count.

items.q: 100 beetles are caught, marked and released. Later 50 are caught and 3 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
Quadrats of 0.50 m² are placed at random in a 500 m² field. The mean is 4.0 plantains per quadrat. Estimate the total number of plantains.
What is environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling?
c: detecting species from DNA left in water or soil
items.e: eDNA can detect platypuses in a creek.

items.q: What is disruptive selection?
c: both extreme phenotypes are favoured over the middle
items.e: It can lead to speciation.

items.q: Which method is used to estimate the population of a mobile animal such as a skink?
items.e: Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂.

items.q: When is a belt transect used?
c: to show how a community changes along an environmental gradient
to measure the age of a tree
to count every organism in a forest
items.e: A transect across a rocky shore shows zonation.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 15, species B 3, species C 3, species D 12, species E 12. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
A quadrat survey found: species A 6, species B 6, species C 4. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).

A quadrat survey found: species A 5, species B 5, species C 12, species D 8, species E 6. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below family?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 15, species B 3, species C 3, species D 3. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below genus?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 2, species B 6, species C 15. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
A quadrat survey found: species A 4, species B 3, species C 4, species D 12, species E 3. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly above kingdom?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species An 8, species B 20, species C 5. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below order?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below class?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

What is genetic diversity?
c: the variety of habitats in a region
the variety of alleles and genes within a species
the number of different species in an area
the number of individuals in a population
items.e: Genetic diversity is variation inside one species.

items.q: 20 fish are caught, marked and released. Later 40 are caught and 10 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
Which definition of a species is used for organisms that reproduce sexually?
c: a group of organisms that look the same
all organisms that live in one habitat
a group that can interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring
a group of organisms with the same diet
items.e: This is the biological species concept.

items.q: A quadrat divided into 25 squares has a species in 10 of them. Calculate the percentage cover (frequency).
A quadrat survey found: species A 10, species B 8, species C 10, species D 20. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
Which assumption is made in capture–mark–recapture?
c: all animals are caught the first time
no animals are born during the whole year
marked animals are easier to catch
marked animals mix back into the population and are not harmed by the mark
items.e: Marks must not affect survival or behaviour.

items.q: Which population is most at risk from a new disease?
c: a population of a widespread species
a small, inbred population with low genetic diversity
a large population with many alleles
items.e: Tasmanian devils have low genetic diversity, which helped facial tumour disease spread.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 20, species B 10, species C 10, species D 2, species E 2. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
A quadrat survey found: species A 4, species B 4, species C 5. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
A quadrat divided into 25 squares has a species in 8 of them. Calculate the percentage cover (frequency).
What are the three domains of life?
items.e: The three-domain system is based on rRNA sequences.

items.q: Why does biodiversity often increase during succession?
c: conditions become less hostile and more niches form
items.e: Biomass also increases.

items.q: Quadrats of 0.25 m² are placed at random in a 200 m² field. The mean is 12 buttercups per quadrat. Estimate the total number of buttercups.
Quadrats of 0.50 m² are placed at random in a 500 m² field. The mean is 3.2 daisies per quadrat. Estimate the total number of daisies.
Why do predator and prey populations rise and fall in cycles?
c: more prey supports more predators, which then reduce the prey
both are limited only by temperature
items.e: Predator peaks lag behind prey peaks.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 20, species B 12, species C 15. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly above class?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: What evidence led to the three-domain system?
c: the shape of cells under a light microscope
items.e: rRNA showed Archaea are as different from Bacteria as from eukaryotes.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 20, species B 6, species C 15, species D 3. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
